text: There's a small fee. She pays it.
Dawn Michelle Hunt, from Chicago, on a trip she thinks she's won.
Waiting to board, she's called aside.
Her brother told lawmakers what she told him.
Her family says she had no idea.
She thought the handbags were a prize.
The bags were checked in her name.
The drugs, she said, were not hers.
Three years later, a court sentences her to death, with a two-year reprieve.
Gene Hunt was, in his son's words, an American of Americans. He had served in the Army, worked as a skimmer in the steel mills, and driven a Chicago bus, before thirty-two years in the police.
As a boy, Tim wrote, he watched his father save the next-door neighbours from a house fire.
There was one person Gene could not bring home.

In May 2025, Tim says, the United States asked for her release on humanitarian grounds. That September, a bipartisan bill was introduced in Congress, named for her and for Nelson Wells Junior, another American held in China.
None of it brought her home.
On January 25th, 2026, four hundred and ninety-four days after that first hearing, Gene Hunt died. He was ninety-two.
